column3: Its accusation of knowing while pursuing a chosen aim loosely parallels knowledge retained but turned into evasion.
It supplies the agency test behind the scene: what is worshiped besides God holds neither harm nor benefit.
The general divine attribute of knowledge does not clarify the reversal or the speechless idols.
Wrongdoers' inability to speak gives a consequential counterpart to the idols' incapacity to speak.
The gift of discernment and light is local background, but it adds little beyond the immediate Abraham argument.
Divine witness to revelation does not materially explain this exchange about idols and self-reversal.
It is the immediate challenge to ask the idols if they speak, which the focus ayah concedes while evading its force.
The blessed reminder and its rejection establish the wider local pattern of refusing disclosed guidance.
Its sequence of clarification before accountability only broadly resembles their rejection after recognition.
Heads lowered before God with an explicit confession forms a strong contrast to the group's inverted retreat from recognized truth.
It is the direct prior moment of inward return and self-indictment that 21:65 immediately reverses.
The restriction of understanding parables to the learned does not add to this narrative scene.
Its fixed, lifted heads portray a distinct judgment-body posture that helps frame the focus's reversal onto heads.
The prohibition of invoking what cannot harm or benefit parallels the practical failure of the speechless objects.
The companions' prudent discussion of duration and provisions does not illuminate the idol confrontation.
Moses' charge that Pharaoh knowingly resists evident signs parallels knowledge preserved within denial.
Fear of the unseen Lord and the Hour supplies only broad moral contrast to the group's response.
Punishment for wrongdoers who do not know gives a general consequence for the injustice they have just admitted.
The declaration of a day when they cannot speak offers a close speechlessness counterpart, though in a different judgment setting.
Ibrahim's granted right guidance and God's knowledge establish the discernment that drives the ensuing exposure.
Deferred knowing after heedless enjoyment only loosely parallels their presently acknowledged knowledge.
The direct challenge, "Why do you not speak?", closely repeats the test that traps the group in 21:65.
It immediately develops the conceded fact into the test of whether their objects can benefit or harm.
God's knowledge of hidden and public speech offers only a broad contrast to their public claim.
The bare introduction of a group's speech adds no distinct help.
Ibrahim's opening question about the images establishes the object of devotion whose speechlessness is later exposed.
Future knowing is too general after the concrete recognition and reversal in the focus.
Punishment poured over heads supplies a judgmental head image, but not the focus's cognitive reversal.
Ibrahim's Creator testimony provides the positive authority opposed to inherited attachment to inert images.
The description of desert dwellers' distance from legal knowledge is not a focused parallel.
The prophetic speech not issuing from desire contrasts with the group's knowingly self-serving utterance.
Its rebuke for worshiping powerless objects and failure to reason is the immediate argumentative conclusion of the focus.
The loss of knowledge in old age shares only a remote reversal motif.
Turning heads away in arrogant refusal supplies a physical and moral analogue to the group's reversal.
The general return and divine report of deeds adds no specific leverage on the scene.
Its warning of future knowledge does not clarify the present knowing concession.
Their head gesture and skeptical question provide another bodily refusal after a resurrection claim.
Their appeal to ancestral worship identifies the social attachment that overturns their brief self-recognition.
The announcement of a knowing son is unrelated to this exchange.
Moses' request for instruction in right guidance offers only distant contrast to refusing known guidance.
The accusation against the idol-breaker begins the public charge that turns back upon the accusers.
Its statement about limited worldly knowledge does not add to this particular recognition.
Individual awareness of deeds at judgment does not clarify the idols' speechlessness.
Ibrahim explicitly names both the group and their forebears as in manifest error, interpreting their inherited defense.
The repeated future warning remains too general to add after earlier cards.
Adam's instruction in names does not illuminate the scene.
The question of what a people worship supplies a parallel opening to an idol inquiry, but is redundant after 21:52.
Comprehensive divine knowledge recorded in a book does not clarify their reversal.
Pharaoh's denial of another god provides a broad example of public theological refusal.
Their uncertainty whether Ibrahim brings truth or play exposes the dismissal that precedes the confrontation.
Seeking refuge from provocation has no material relation to this scene.
The call to spend and warning of replacement do not clarify the idols or the response.
Public identification of Ibrahim adds procedural context but little after the charge is established.
Personal awareness of what one has brought does not add to the focus.
The same reversal root in bodily aging gives a limited formal parallel without the focus's social and cognitive movement.
The group's settled devotion to idols is a redundant general counterpart to the local ancestral worship.
God's knowledge of what people invoke besides Him supports the broader exposure of false devotion.
Its indictment of contradictory conduct offers a broad analogue to acting against an acknowledged judgment.
Ibrahim's announced plan against the idols sets up the shattered evidence that precipitates the group's self-testimony.
General knowledge of the unseen and deeds does not clarify the focus.
The community's repentance after hardship is not a useful parallel to this reversal.
The order to bring Ibrahim before public eyes adds only procedural detail beyond the accusation.
The greeting upon Noah does not illuminate the focus scene.
The statement of God's absolute ownership and power is too broad here.
The question whether idols hear those who invoke them closely supports the speech-and-agency test.
Teaching scripture and wisdom does not add to the scene.
Turning backs in battlefield panic provides only a distant physical reversal parallel.
The smashing of the idols is the decisive evidence arranged to make the people return to reflection.
A known appointed measure does not clarify the focus.
Sealed mouths while limbs speak reverses ordinary speech and gives a judgmental counterpart to the silent idols.
The direct public accusation of Ibrahim is already supplied by the surrounding local sequence.
Provision for creatures does not illuminate this argument.
The awakening to distinguish duration calculations does not add to the focus.
Grasping a head in anger supplies only a remote bodily-head resonance.
Election upon knowledge is unrelated to the group's reversal.
Signs made clear to people who know broadly contrasts with this refusal to follow evident proof.
The command to burn Ibrahim shows the group's active defense of the exposed idols after their retreat from recognition.
A claim made without knowledge, inherited from forebears, closely contrasts with their admission that the idols do not speak.
Persistence in rebellion even after relief supplies a general pattern of refusing corrective disclosure.
The calf's inability to return speech or control harm and benefit is a close parallel, though later than the more direct local cards.
The rebuke for teaching God one's religion does not specifically advance the idol scene.
Human ownership of livestock does not bear on the focus.
The fire's reversal into safety completes the local counter-reversal after the group's hostile response.
Speculation without knowledge is a loose contrast to refusing an admitted fact.
Inability to move forward or return at a place does not clarify the focus's reversal.
Hearing without receiving reason offers a broad structural analogy to the failed call for reflection.
The relation of human and divine willing does not add to this scene.
Calling associates who do not answer before punishment gives a close crisis counterpart to the powerless idols.
The failure of their plot is local aftermath but adds little to the focus's argument.
Noah's refusal to judge hidden deeds does not illuminate this exchange.
Lot's offer of his daughters is unrelated.
Deferred knowledge after ingratitude is too general and redundant.
Mutual questioning in the hereafter does not clarify the focus scene.
Clear signs rejected only by wrongdoers broadly frames their resistance to the displayed evidence.
A revived observer recognizing divine power provides only a distant contrast to their refusal of evident proof.
Qarun's self-attribution to knowledge gives a general case of knowledge used in self-serving denial.
Pharaoh's question about the Lord of the worlds does not add to the focus.
Post-knowledge disagreement among Israel does not clarify this narrative exchange.
Rules concerning residence, maintenance, and nursing are unrelated.
The discovery of the sleepers confirms resurrection but does not help explain the idols' speechlessness or reversal.
The calf cannot speak to or guide its worshipers, making it an especially close independent parallel to the exposed idols of 21:65.
The calf-worshipers' remorse and recognition that they had gone astray closely parallel the brief self-recognition before the focus's reversal.
The calf's merely sounding body clarifies the difference between producing a sound and answering speech, directly sharpening the test in 21:65.
The question whether idols can benefit or harm completes the same agency test introduced by their inability to hear invocation.
Those invoked besides God cannot answer their callers and are unaware of the invocation, a direct broader analogue to speechless idols.
The inventory of idols' missing bodily capacities develops the same exposure of objects unable to act or respond.
Worship of what can neither harm nor benefit provides a concise doctrinal counterpart to the local idol test.
Those called besides God create nothing and are themselves created, reinforcing the objects' lack of independent agency.
Invoked beings cannot remove or alter harm, extending the consequence of their inability to speak or act.
False gods neither create nor control death, life, or resurrection, giving a wider account of the power denied by the focus.
Those called besides God possess no share or authority, supplying a broader authority test for the exposed idols.
The invoked cannot hear and would not answer even if they heard, closely articulating the failed-address dimension of the focus.
Gods taken for hoped-for aid cannot help their worshipers, adding the failed expectation behind attachment to inert objects.
Ibrahim's approach to the idols supplies adjacent narrative context for the challenge about their silence, but 37:92 already carries the decisive question.
